questions.q: What is the main advantage and the main limitation of rolling back a change during an incident?
options: It has no advantages — fixing forward is always the better choice
It's fast and returns the system to a known-good state, but it doesn't fix the underlying root cause
It always fixes the root cause permanently, but takes longer than fixing forward
It is only possible in non-production environments
questions.explain: A rollback is usually a fast, low-risk way to restore service, but the underlying issue (the stale rule, missing permission, etc.) is still there waiting to resurface.

questions.q: What is the main advantage and the main cost of fixing forward during an incident?
options: It never actually resolves the underlying cause
It addresses the root cause directly, but takes longer and carries more risk of introducing a second problem mid-incident
It is always faster than a rollback and carries no additional risk
It can only be done after the incident is fully over
questions.explain: Fixing forward resolves the actual problem in place, but diagnosing fully and applying a correct fix under pressure takes more time and carries more risk than a rollback.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which factor should push a team toward rolling back rather than fixing forward?
options: The fix isn't fully understood or tested yet, and a large portion of a production system is currently down
The environment is a low-stakes staging or dev environment
The root cause and the fix are both small and clearly identified
The change would lose other unrelated work already shipped
questions.explain: When the fix is uncertain and the business impact of continued downtime is high, the safer, faster path is usually to roll back first and diagnose properly afterward.

questions.q: In the Lesson 32 example, why did fixing forward make more sense than rolling back the entire deployment?
options: Because rolling back was technically impossible in that environment
Because the root cause was never actually identified
Because the incident happened in a staging environment with no real stakes
Because the fix was small, well-understood, and low-risk — a one-line correction to a single existing rule's source IP range
questions.explain: A small, well-understood, low-blast-radius fix is exactly the case this lesson says favors fixing forward over rolling back an entire deployment.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say neither rolling back nor fixing forward is automatically "the more professional" choice?
options: Because rolling back is always unprofessional in a production environment
Because fixing forward is always required by best practice
Because the right choice depends on reading the specific situation's stakes and certainty, not on always preferring one approach
Because the choice has no real consequences either way
questions.explain: Treating one approach as always correct is a common mistake — restoring service quickly with a rollback, then fixing forward properly afterward, is often the right professional call.
